Nysa New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Nysa, Poland

Not demolished. Jews are first recorded in Nysa in 1319, building a wooden synagogue in 1410 before a 1468 De Non Tolerandis Judeis ban took effect. A community revival began in the early 19th century; land for a synagogue was purchased in 1838, and population reached 464 by 1861 before declining sharply to 220 (0.6%) by 1932 amid westward emigration. Following Kristallnacht, some Jews left; in July 1942, Nysa's remaining Jews were deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau. This newer cemetery, established in 1815 near Catholic and Evangelical cemeteries, was enlarged in 1871; its last known burial occurred in 1928. Ownership transferred to the Reich Association of Jews in Germany in 1939, then to the Gestapo in June 1943; WWII brought devastation that continued postwar. Authorities formally closed the cemetery to burials in 1967, when about 100 damaged tombstones remained; roughly 25 broken matzevot survive today, some bearing German and Hebrew inscriptions, alongside remnants of the original brick-post fence and a preserved central alley outline.
